paragraphs.heading: Finding planets indirectly
paragraphs.text: Most ways of finding planets around other stars are indirect: instead of taking a picture of the planet, astronomers work out that it is there from some other signal. That is because a planet gives off very little light next to its star. A star like the Sun outshines the light reflected by its planets about a billion times over, and the star's glare washes them out. So by June 2025, only a few of the planets reported had been seen directly.

paragraphs.heading: Watching for a dip
paragraphs.text: The transit method is one of these indirect ways. When a planet crosses, or transits, in front of the disk of its star, the star looks a little dimmer to us. How much dimmer depends on how big the planet is compared with the star. So while the radial-velocity method tells astronomers about a planet's mass, this photometric method, which works from the star's brightness, can reveal its radius.

paragraphs.heading: How small the dips are
paragraphs.text: The size of the dip varies a lot. The star HD 209458 fades by 1.7% when its planet passes in front. Most dips are far smaller: an Earth-size planet crossing a Sun-like star dims it by just 80 parts per million, which is 0.008 percent.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the light curve
paragraphs.text: A model of a transiting planet's light curve predicts four things: the transit depth (δ), the transit duration (T), the ingress and egress duration (τ), and the planet's period (P). The transit depth is how much the star's normalized flux falls during the transit. These numbers rest on simplifying assumptions: the planet and star are treated as spheres, the star's disk as evenly bright, and the orbit as a circle. The shape of the measured curve also changes depending on where the planet sits as it crosses the star.

paragraphs.heading: Working with radial velocity
paragraphs.text: The transit method pairs well with the radial-velocity method. That method tracks how a star speeds up and slows down toward and away from Earth as it moves in a small orbit under a planet's pull. Radial velocity can be used to confirm planets that transits turn up. On its own it gives only a planet's minimum mass, but when both methods are used together, astronomers can estimate the planet's true mass.
